title: Forgetting in prayer
hook: two prostrations at the end if you forget

segments.voice: Yesterday, qasr: the four-unit prayers shortened to two on the road. Today, a prayer that comes out short by accident.

An afternoon prayer in Medina. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ leads it, and ends it after two units. A four-unit prayer, finished at two. He goes and leans against a piece of wood in the mosque. People stand around, uneasy. Then a man the companions nicknamed Dhul-Yadayn, the one with the long hands, asks: has the prayer been shortened, or did you forget? Neither, as far as he knows, he answers, and he turns to the others. Is it true? It's true. So he goes back, prays what he left out, and adds today's word at the end.
screen: `FOUR UNITS, ENDED AT TWO.` → `THE MAN WITH THE LONG HANDS.` → `SHORTENED, OR FORGOTTEN?`

segments.voice: Sujud al-sahw means the prostrations of forgetfulness: two extra prostrations near the end of the prayer, made when something was added, left out, or is in doubt. First, that story, from Sahih al-Bukhari. Nobody was shamed. The prayer wasn't thrown out. The missing units were prayed, and two prostrations mended it. Second, what the Prophet said about himself. Another report in Bukhari has him say, after a slip in prayer: I am only a human being like you. I forget as you forget. So when I forget, remind me. That line comes from the one who had just led the prayer. Third, doubt. A hadith in Sahih Muslim gives a familiar case: you can't remember whether you've prayed three units or four. Throw the doubt away, it says, and build on what you're sure of, then make two prostrations before you finish. Not start over. Not stand there replaying it. Fourth, where the schools differ: whether the two prostrations come before the closing salam or after it. The Hanafi school places them after. The Shafi'i school places them before. The Maliki school depends on whether something was added or left out, and the Hanbali school follows the specific report for each case. They agree on the main thing: the prayer comes with its own repair kit.
screen: `ENDED EARLY, THEN MENDED.` · `I FORGET AS YOU FORGET.` · `BUILD ON WHAT YOU'RE SURE OF.` · `BEFORE THE SALAM, OR AFTER?` · then, large: `WHEN I FORGET, REMIND ME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small mistake from this week, a forgotten call, a missed step, a word in the wrong place, and see it without replaying it; then picture one small step that would mend it, and let the replaying go on the out-breath. If you pray, remember the two prostrations next time you lose count, and mend the prayer rather than abandon it. If you don't, simply set the mistake down, and leave it there.
Sujud al-sahw. The prostrations of forgetfulness: two prostrations near the end of the prayer that mend a slip. Today's word.
Your line: mistakes are expected. Even the Prophet said: I forget as you forget. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: When Muslims add to, leave out, or lose count in a prayer, they make two extra prostrations near its end, before or after the closing salam depending on their school, and the prayer stands.

notes: Editor: 'from inside the prayer itself' corrected (in Bukhari 401 he says it after turning to the people, having just led the prayer); cut the unsourced 'forgetting was expected from the start'; practice changed from 'what am I sure of?' (close to day 1075's practice) to naming one mending step.

Bukhari 482 (Dhul-Yadayn): the report says one of the two afternoon prayers (zuhr or asr) ended after two rak'ahs; the Prophet leaned on a piece of wood; he said he had neither forgotten nor had it been shortened (in some wordings 'I did not forget and it was not shortened'). 'As far as he knows' is the writer's softening; confirm.

Bukhari 401 (Ibn Mas'ud: 'I am only a human being like you; I forget as you forget, so when I forget, remind me') paraphrased; Muslim 571 (Abu Sa'id: doubt between three and four) paraphrased. Confirm numbers.
Fiqh summary of placement: Hanafi after salam; Shafi'i before; Maliki before for omission, after for addition; Hanbali per the reported case (generally before). Confirm.
Some omissions (of a pillar) require making up the unit, not only the two prostrations; the script says 'mend' and the myth avoids 'every slip'. Keeper may wish to add a line.
Bukhari 482 also names Abu Bakr and Umar as present and hesitant to speak; left out for length.
